text: Redis Pub/Sub has at-most-once delivery: if a subscriber is disconnected or fails to handle a message, that message is lost for good. Redis Streams persist messages and support at-least-once delivery when that is needed.
why: Names the exact guarantee and the Redis alternative with persistence.

text: Since Redis 7.0, sharded Pub/Sub (SSUBSCRIBE/SPUBLISH) keeps a message within one shard of a cluster; classic Pub/Sub propagates every message to every node, which limits how far it scales.
why: Relevant when the inter-edge-server Pub/Sub is a clustered Redis, as on the board.

text: Slack's own description (2023): the client sends a message through the HTTP Webapp API; a Channel Server chosen by consistent hashing fans it out to every Gateway Server subscribed to that channel, and Gateway Servers hold the clients' WebSocket connections in multiple regions.
why: Real-world confirmation of 'send over HTTP, receive over WebSocket'.

text: Slack's 2020 Vitess post explains that its original databases were sharded by workspace id, and that with Vitess it wanted to shard message data by channel id because that spreads the load much more evenly.
why: Shows the channel_id shard key is the one Slack itself aimed for.

text: WhatsApp deletes messages from its servers once delivered; an undelivered message is held encrypted on its servers for up to 30 days while delivery is retried, then deleted.
why: Explains how offline delivery works without server-side history.

text: Alternatives to WebSocket for receiving: Server-Sent Events give a one-way server-to-client stream over HTTP, and HTTP long polling holds the request open until there is new data. Short polling is what gives the poor real-time UX.
why: Shows WebSocket is the usual choice, not the only one.

text: HTTP/1.1 uses persistent connections by default, so repeated REST calls usually reuse one TCP/TLS connection instead of handshaking each time.
why: Removes the student's main argument against REST for sending.

text: QUIC, the transport under HTTP/3, runs over UDP datagrams and builds its own reliable delivery and congestion control on top. UDP itself guarantees nothing; reliability has to be added above it.
why: Prevents the misreading that UDP-based always means lossy.

text: Kafka consumers can reprocess records: if a consumer crashes after processing a batch but before saving its offset, its replacement reads them again. Writes keyed by a unique message id turn that redelivery into a harmless overwrite.
why: The async persistence worker must be idempotent.

text: Kafka does not delete messages when they are consumed; it keeps them for a configured time- or size-based retention window, so consumers can re-read history within that window.
why: Clarifies what 'persistence of historical messages' means in Kafka.

text: Slack's message 'ts' value is essentially the message ID and is guaranteed unique within a channel or conversation, giving one server-assigned order per channel.
why: Real example of server-assigned ordering ids.

text: Zoom offers continuous meeting chat: when enabled, meeting messages live on in Zoom's persistent chat before, during and after the meeting. Without it, participants see only messages sent while they are present.
why: The Zoom example depends on the setting.

text: A vector clock holds one counter per process and gives a partial causal order: it can say message A happened before B, or that they were concurrent, but it does not by itself order concurrent messages.
why: Corrects the idea that vector clocks give a single 'true' order.

text: WhatsApp completed its rollout of the Signal Protocol for end-to-end encryption in April 2016, covering one-to-one chats, group chats, attachments, voice notes and calls.
why: Confirms the teacher's Signal remark with a dated source.

text: Apache Parquet is an open-source, column-oriented file format with compression and encoding schemes built for efficient bulk storage and retrieval, which is why warehouses and lakes favour it.
why: Gives the 'go look up Parquet' homework a starting point.

text: In the 1945 EDVAC report von Neumann modelled his logic 'E elements' on McCulloch and Pitts' 1943 model of the neuron, built as digital vacuum-tube gates.
why: Grounds the brain analogy in the real history.
